Explain the real decision-0005 finding: Program.cs registers IClockEntryRepository as Singleton but IClockEntryService, PayrollService, and IEmployeeService as Transient -- and why that mix is safe for this specific console app.

preQuiz.prompt: What do Mock<IClockEntryRepository>() and RecordingRepository : IClockEntryRepository have in common as test doubles?
options: Both are objects that implement the real IClockEntryRepository interface, letting a test control GetEmployeeClockEntries/GetClockEntry/SaveClockEntry's behavior without touching the real, in-memory ClockEntryRepository
Nothing -- they are unrelated testing techniques
Both require the real database to be running
preQuiz.explanation: The mechanism differs (Moq generates an implementation at runtime; RecordingRepository is a small class written by hand), but the underlying principle -- substituting an interface implementation for testing -- is identical.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does Program.cs register IClockEntryRepository as Singleton while IClockEntryService is Transient?
options: ClockEntryRepository holds the actual state (_clockEntries) that ClockIn and Clockout both need to share across calls; ClockEntryService itself holds no state of its own, so a new instance per resolution costs nothing and shares the same underlying (Singleton) repository anyway
It is an arbitrary, unexplained inconsistency
Transient services cannot depend on Singleton services
preQuiz.explanation: decision-0005 documents this as real and verified against the actual Program.cs: the lifetime choice tracks which class actually needs shared state, not a uniform policy.

preQuiz.prompt: What does AddScoped<EntryRecorder>() guarantee within a single IServiceScope?
options: Every GetRequiredService<EntryRecorder>() call within that one scope returns the SAME EntryRecorder instance; a different scope gets a different instance
A new instance every single call, scope or not
Exactly one instance for the entire application's lifetime
preQuiz.explanation: Scoped is the real middle ground between Transient (always new) and Singleton (always the same) -- ServiceCompositionTests.cs demonstrates this directly with two different scopes.

concept.title: Two real test-double mechanisms in this codebase
paragraphs: Session 28's PayrollServiceTests.cs uses Moq: new Mock<IClockEntryRepository>() generates an implementation at runtime, configured with .Setup(...).Returns(...).
EntryRecorderTests.cs's RecordingRepository is hand-written: a small, real private class implementing every member of IClockEntryRepository directly, tracking what was saved in a simple property.

concept.title: The real, mixed DI lifetimes, and why they are safe here
paragraphs: decision-0005, verified directly against the real Program.cs: IClockEntryRepository is Singleton (one shared instance, holding the real _clockEntries state); IClockEntryService, PayrollService, and IEmployeeService are all Transient (a new instance every resolution).

This mix is safe specifically because ClockEntryService and PayrollService hold no mutable state of their own -- every Transient instance simply forwards to the one shared Singleton repository, so creating a new service instance costs a small allocation and nothing more.

concept.title: Scoped: the lifetime this console app never needed, but ASP.NET Core will
paragraphs: ServiceComposition.AddTimeClockCore registers EntryRecorder as Scoped -- one instance per IServiceScope, demonstrated by ServiceCompositionTests.cs resolving it twice within one scope (same instance) and once in a second scope (a different instance).

Scoped becomes directly relevant once Session 32's ASP.NET Core WebApi is built: ASP.NET Core creates one scope per HTTP request automatically, so a Scoped registration there means one instance per request -- a pattern this console app, with no request boundary, never needed until now.

lab.objective: Compare Moq-based and hand-written test doubles for IClockEntryRepository, and confirm all three real DI lifetimes (Transient, Singleton, Scoped) behave as documented.
lab.startingCondition: PayrollServiceTests.cs (Moq), EntryRecorderTests.cs (hand-written RecordingRepository), and ServiceCompositionTests.cs (Scoped) already exist.
steps: Read RecordingRepository's four interface members and compare its line count and readability to the equivalent Mock<IClockEntryRepository> setup in PayrollServiceTests.cs.
Resolve IClockEntryService twice from the same ServiceProvider and confirm you get two different (Transient) instances.
Resolve IClockEntryRepository twice from the same ServiceProvider and confirm you get the SAME (Singleton) instance.
Run ServiceCompositionTests.cs and confirm EntryRecorder is the same instance within one scope but different across two scopes.
lab.expectedBehavior: Both test-double styles work correctly for their respective tests; Transient/Singleton/Scoped each demonstrate their documented, distinct behavior when resolved directly from a ServiceProvider.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

commit: session-29: teach test doubles di lifetimes and service tests
review: Both real test-double mechanisms (Moq and hand-written) are compared directly, not treated as interchangeable without discussion.
decision-0005's real, mixed DI lifetimes are explained by what state each class holds, not applied as an unexplained rule.
Scoped lifetime is demonstrated with the real ServiceCompositionTests.cs assertions, and connected forward to Session 32's ASP.NET Core per-request scoping.

postQuiz.prompt: Why would registering IClockEntryRepository as Transient (instead of the real Singleton) break ClockIn/Clockout's real behavior in Program.cs?
options: Each resolution would get a fresh, empty _clockEntries list -- ClockIn's saved entry would live in a different repository instance than the one Clockout later queries, so Clockout would never find it
Nothing would break -- Transient and Singleton behave identically for this class
It would cause a compile error
postQuiz.explanation: This is exactly the scenario Session 19's lab explored -- Singleton is what lets ClockIn and Clockout share the same underlying state across two separate method calls.

postQuiz.prompt: When would you choose a hand-written fake like RecordingRepository over a Moq-based mock?
options: When the interface is small and the fake's behavior is simple enough that hand-writing it is clearer and has no extra library dependency -- both are legitimate choices, and this codebase genuinely uses both
Never -- Moq should always be preferred
Hand-written fakes are only valid for interfaces with one member
postQuiz.explanation: There is no universal rule -- IClockEntryRepository's real test suite uses both approaches in different tests, which is itself the honest answer: it depends on the specific test's needs.

postQuiz.prompt: If ClockEntryService.Clockout were called from two different HTTP requests handled concurrently by the real WebApi project (Session 32), and IClockEntryRepository stayed registered as Singleton there too, what real risk would that introduce?
options: Concurrent requests could race on the same shared, mutable _clockEntries list with no synchronization -- a genuine risk this codebase's real, single-threaded console app never had to face
No risk -- Singleton services are always thread-safe automatically
The WebApi would fail to start
postQuiz.explanation: This is a real, forward-looking risk worth naming honestly: Singleton state that was safe in a single-threaded console app becomes a genuine concurrency concern once multiple requests can run in parallel.

reflections: Why does this codebase's test suite use two different test-double styles (Moq and hand-written) instead of standardizing on one?
What would you need to verify before trusting that IClockEntryRepository's real Singleton registration is still safe once the WebApi project (Session 32) starts handling concurrent requests?
Where might Scoped be a better fit than Transient or Singleton for a class this codebase doesn't have yet?
whatBreaks: Registering IClockEntryRepository as Transient instead of Singleton breaks the real ClockIn-then-Clockout sequence, because each resolution would receive an independent, empty _clockEntries list. Using Moq for every single test double, even trivially simple ones, adds a library dependency and a layer of setup-call indirection where a five-line hand-written fake like RecordingRepository would be just as clear. Assuming Singleton services are automatically safe under concurrent access ignores a real risk that becomes relevant the moment this codebase gains a multi-request host (Session 32).
summary: This codebase's real test suite uses two legitimate test-double styles side by side: Moq (Session 28's PayrollServiceTests.cs) and hand-written fakes (EntryRecorderTests.cs's RecordingRepository) -- both satisfy IClockEntryRepository, by different mechanisms. decision-0005's real, mixed Transient/Singleton registrations in Program.cs are safe specifically because only ClockEntryRepository holds shared state; ServiceComposition's Scoped example previews a third lifetime this console app never needed but Session 32's ASP.NET Core WebApi (one scope per request) will.
